rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Centripetal acceleration (a_c = v²/r = rω²) is directed toward the centre of a circular path. The centripetal force (F_c = mv²/r) is the resultant of real forces (tension, gravity, friction) — not a new force. Maximum-speed problems (string breaking, car skidding) and identifying which real force provides F_c are the key NEB topics.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Centripetal acceleration: $a_c = v^2/r = r\omega^2$ (directed toward the centre)
Centripetal force: $F_c = mv^2/r = mr\omega^2$ (resultant of real forces toward centre)
Maximum speed (string): $v_{max} = \sqrt{T_{max} \times r/m}$ — when tension reaches breaking point

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Inertial/Non-Inertial Distinction:** Centripetal force is a real resultant force in an inertial frame; it is not a 'fictitious' force. Fictitious centrifugal force only appears in the rotating reference frame to maintain Newton's laws.  ·  **Directional Constraint:** Centripetal force must act strictly perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity for the speed to remain constant. If the net force has a tangential component, the speed changes (non-uniform circular motion).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Always identify which real force provides the centripetal force — never add 'centripetal force' as a separate force in the FBD.  ·  Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force — it appears only in rotating reference frames, not in inertial frames.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Car turning: A 1200 kg car turns a flat curve of radius 60 m at 15 m/s. F_c = 1200 × 225/60 = 4500 N (provided by friction).  ·  Ball on string: A 0.3 kg ball on a 2 m string rotates at 6 m/s. Tension = 0.3 × 36/2 = 5.4 N.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ 'Centrifugal force pulls the body outward.' ✅ Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force that appears only in a rotating reference frame. In an inertial frame, there is only centripetal force toward the centre.  ·  ❌ 'Centripetal force is a new type of force.' ✅ Centripetal force is the RESULTANT of real forces (tension, gravity, friction). It is not a separate force you add to the FBD.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 problems calculating centripetal force/acceleration for different scenarios.  ·  Solve 5 maximum-speed problems (string breaking, car skidding) using F_c = mv²/r.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Force identification trick: always ask 'which real force points toward the centre?' — that's your F_c.  ·  Maximum speed shortcut: v_max = √(μ_s rg) for flat curves, v_max = √(T_max r/m) for strings.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: A 1500 kg car turns a flat curve of radius 80 m at 25 m/s. Find the minimum coefficient of friction needed to prevent skidding.  ·  A 0.6 kg ball on a 2 m string rotates at 5 m/s. Find the tension. If the string breaks at 12 N, find the maximum speed.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Maximum-speed problems (string breaking, car skidding) are the most common type.  ·  Always identify which real force provides the centripetal force — never add it as a separate force.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Centripetal acceleration (a_c = v²/r = rω²) is directed toward the centre of the circular path.  ·  Centripetal force is the resultant of real forces pointing toward the centre — it is not a new force.  ·  Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force that appears only in rotating reference frames.  ·  If the centripetal force is removed, the body moves tangent to the circle.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Centripetal force is NOT a new force — it is the resultant of real forces (tension, gravity, friction).  ·  Centripetal acceleration changes only the direction of velocity, not its magnitude.  ·  Centripetal force is proportional to v² — doubling speed quadruples the required force.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Centripetal force is not a new force — it is the resultant of real forces pointing toward the centre.  ·  The direction of centripetal acceleration is always toward the centre — it changes velocity direction, not magnitude.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: A satellite orbits Earth at 7 km/s at a radius of 6800 km. Find the centripetal acceleration.  ·  A cyclist turns a curve of radius 30 m at 12 m/s. At what angle must the cyclist lean to avoid falling?  ·  Explain why passengers feel pushed outward when a car takes a sharp turn, and identify the real forces involved.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force — use it only in rotating reference frames.  ·  Cyclist lean angle problems: tan θ = v²/(rg) — a classic NEB question.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Planet orbit: A satellite orbits Earth at 8 km/s at a radius of 7000 km. a_c = (8000)²/(7×10⁶) = 9.14 m/s².  ·  Maximum speed: A 0.4 kg ball on a 1.5 m string (max tension 15 N). v_max = √(15 × 1.5/0.4) = 7.5 m/s.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: A 1000 kg car turns a flat curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. The minimum coefficient of friction to prevent skidding is: (g = 10 m/s²) → C  ·  A 0.5 kg ball on a 1.5 m string rotates at 4 m/s. The tension is: → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Centripetal acceleration (a_c):** the acceleration directed toward the centre of a circular path that keeps a body moving in a circle. Magnitude: a_c = v²/r = rω². Direction: always toward the centre (hence 'centripetal' = 'centre-seeking'). It changes the direction of velocity, not its magnitude.  ·  **Centripetal force (F_c):** the net force required to produce centripetal acceleration: F_c = mv²/r = mrω². It is NOT a new force — it is the RESULTANT of real forces (tension, gravity, friction, normal) pointing toward the centre.  ·  **Why centripetal force is not a separate force:** the centripetal force is always provided by one or more real forces. For a car turning on a flat road, friction provides F_c. For a planet orbiting the Sun, gravity provides F_c. For a ball on a string, tension provides F_c.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Centripetal force is proportional to v² — doubling the speed quadruples the required force.  ·  Maximum speed (flat curve): $v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu_s rg}$ — when friction reaches its maximum  ·  Cyclist lean angle: $\tan \theta = v^2/(rg)$ — the angle needed to balance torque

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Radius Variation:** If the path radius $r$ changes during the motion, the centripetal force requirement $F_c = mv^2/r$ must adjust instantaneously based on the new radius and speed at that instant.  ·  ❌ 'The body in circular motion is in equilibrium.' ✅ The body accelerates toward the centre (a_c = v²/r). It is NOT in equilibrium — the net force is mv²/r toward the centre.  ·  ❌ 'Centripetal acceleration changes the speed.' ✅ Centripetal acceleration changes only the DIRECTION of velocity. Tangential acceleration (if present) changes the speed.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ 'Centripetal force acts outward.' ✅ Centripetal force acts INWARD, toward the centre. The tendency to move outward is inertia, not a force.  ·  ❌ 'If the string breaks, the body moves radially outward.' ✅ If the string breaks, the body moves TANGENT to the circle (in the direction of its velocity at that instant), not radially.  ·  Conical pendulum: A 0.2 kg bob rotates at 3 m/s in a horizontal circle of radius 0.8 m. F_c = 0.2 × 9/0.8 = 2.25 N.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: If the centripetal force is removed, the body moves tangent to the circle (Newton's first law).  ·  Maximum-speed problems: set F_c = mv²/r equal to the maximum available force (tension, friction) and solve for v.  ·  NEB frequently asks: 'Find the maximum speed' — use v_max = √(μ_s rg) for curves, v_max = √(T_max r/m) for strings.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Centrifugal force is a pseudo-force — it appears only in rotating reference frames.  ·  Maximum-speed problems: set F_c = mv²/r equal to the maximum available force and solve for v.  ·  Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the centre of the circular path: a_c = v²/r = rω².
